source.title: SessionRec: Next Session Prediction Paradigm For Generative Sequential Recommendation
source.authors: Lei Huang; Hao Guo; Lin-Zhi Peng; Long Zhang; Xiaoteng Wang; Daoyuan Wang; Shi-Chao Wang; Jin-Peng Wang; Lei Wang; Sheng Chen

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling in generative sequential recommendation, a different setting from language-model pretraining, and reports a data-volume scaling result.
record.gate_note: The paper cites LLM scaling laws as motivation, but cited findings are not rows. Its own relevant result is the Meituan data-volume scaling experiment. It does not sweep model parameters, training tokens or compute, or measure held-out cross-entropy loss.
record.test_reason: The only scaling result is Figure 5. It varies training data for a recommendation model (SessionRec-HSTU) and measures Recall@500, a retrieval metric, not held-out loss. The fitted curve is logarithmic (y=0.0383·ln(x)−0.348) over about one decade of data (0.4–4×10^11 items). Model size and compute are not varied or quantified. This is a related but different construct, so it cannot show whether V5's power-law loss form holds. It is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with one correction. The authors claim SessionRec shows 'clear power-law scaling laws similar to those observed in LLMs'. Their evidence is a single curve: Recall@500 rises linearly with exponentially more data, fitted logarithmically. They do not fit a power law, do not vary model size, and do not quantify compute.
record.recipe_differences: Measures Recall@500 for a recommendation model while varying training data volume; it does not measure held-out language-model loss or sweep model parameters, tokens and compute.

fits_no_version.finding: For SessionRec-HSTU on Meituan data, Recall@500 rises roughly linearly in ln(training items) between about 0.4 and 4×10^11 items. The fit is y=0.0383·ln(x)−0.348. Data are figure only, with no uncertainty and one model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generative sequential recommenders' retrieval recall improves log-linearly with training data volume.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code will be made publicly available.
record.problems: The scaling result is reported for one model backbone, one industrial dataset and one retrieval metric. Exact plotted observations and uncertainty estimates are not reported in the text, and the stated fitted curve is logarithmic rather than a power law.
record.rows_left_out: No other results bear on the listed claim versions: the other experiments compare recommendation accuracy, session aggregation methods, rank-loss weights or online business metrics, rather than the specified scaling-law outcomes.

untested.parts: No shape-at-fixed-parameter comparison. The layer and head ablations in Table 4 concern the session encoder and do not hold parameter count fixed.
Untested: power-law loss in recommendation, and image/video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer. Only recall versus data size is reported.

record.verdict_notes: The power-law claim in the abstract is not matched by the reported logarithmic fit on a recall metric. The study is a recommendation-method paper whose scaling section is a brief, figure-only result. The reader's 'challenges' verdict on V5 was removed because the measure cannot bear on power-law loss.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss or sweep over parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep over parameter count and tokens.
No comparison of language-model depth, width or architecture at fixed parameter count.
Tests only recommendation-model performance versus training data volume; it does not test image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
No downstream-task performance relationship with language-model scale or pretraining loss.
Does not compare fitting choices or report that setup choices alter fitted exponents or cause curves to bend.

rows.subject: SessionRec-HSTU
rows.size_stated: Model parameter count not stated; dataset covers approximately 400 million users.
rows.operation_detail: Varied training data volume, quantified by the number of items in training sequences, and measured retrieval performance.

conditions.value: Large-scale industrial dataset from the Meituan App

rows.value: Fitted Curve: y=0.03829156*ln(x)-0.348426; plotted data values are figure only.
rows.note: The text says performance increases as training data volume and computing power increase. The plotted fit is logarithmic in training data size; exact plotted observations are not stated in the text.
rows.check: The measure is Recall@500 of a recommender, not loss, and the fit is log-linear rather than a power law. It spans only about 10x in data with one model size and no uncertainty, so it cannot confirm or refute V5's power-law loss form. The reader's 'partial' state and 'challenges' label overreach: a log-linear recall curve is not evidence against power-law loss. Baseline is correctly 'not stated'. Figure 5's y-axis spans roughly 0.58–0.66.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5, lines 1454–1467; Figure 5 fit equation, line 1513.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

rows.locator_found: Section 5, lines 1454–1467; Figure 5 fit equation, line 1513.

relation.reason: The authors explicitly compare their recommendation scaling curve with LLM scaling laws, but their reported measurements do not test a listed version.

tranche.reason: The data-volume sweep measures recommendation Recall@500 with a logarithmic fit. It does not measure the power-law loss, extrapolation, allocation, architecture, downstream-transfer or fitting-dependence effects specified by the claim versions.

source_check.notes: Figure 5 explicitly gives y=0.03829156*ln(x)-0.348426; exact plotted observations are not stated. The authors describe power-law scaling, but the displayed fit is logarithmic, and computing power is mentioned without quantitative measurements.
